problem: MLLM-based frontier exploration agents rely on stale pre-trained knowledge, explore statelessly without cross-episode experience, and must rank dozens of visually similar frontier snapshots, which is unreliable and costly. RL-style training to learn from experience is expensive given long horizons and sparse rewards.
motivation: Humans reflect on past successes and failures in hindsight and reuse the lessons in new environments. The authors ask whether an MLLM agent can gain reusable exploration experience non-parametrically at inference time. Large flat frontier sets also overwhelm open-source MLLMs.
key_idea: Distill completed exploration trajectories into abstract outcome-aware textual experiences, retrieve them by scene and task similarity to condition frontier selection at inference time, and make frontier choice coarse-to-fine through hierarchical (broad-view then close-up-view) selection.
insight: Abstracted experience acts as a strategic prior, e.g. go through hallways to reach functional zones and avoid dead ends. Removing replay drops GPT-4o LLM-Match from 58.3 to 50.6 and Qwen from 46.2 to 40.3. Hierarchical selection beats listwise, pointwise and pairwise ranking on Qwen (LLM-Match 42.1 vs 34.2 for listwise), and the gap widens as the number of frontiers grows (listwise wins only at about 6 frontiers). Salient recall beats random retrieval, and high-quality abstractions beat low-quality ones (both shown only in figures).
method: Trajectory Verbalization: converts each step's state and chosen frontier into text, groups every 10 steps into a chunk caption, and merges chunk captions into a trajectory caption (Qwen-based captioner).

Retrospective Reflection and Abstraction: given the outcome, a self-reflection prompt covers task-level, environment-level and hypothetical reflection, then CoT distillation produces a scene-agnostic abstraction (a 20-24 sentence paragraph in the prompt, described as two paragraphs in the text).

Salient Experience Recall: embeds frontier snapshots with OpenCLIP ViT-H/14 and questions with MiniLM-L6-v2, ranks trajectories by scene and task similarity, fuses them with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (k=60), and injects the top-5 abstractions into the prompt.
Working Memory: an episode-bounded text summary of the last 5 chosen frontier snapshots (regions visited, cues, uncertain directions) added to the prompt.

Hierarchical Frontier Selection: two-stage K-means (k<=3) over frontier points gives Broad-View Frontiers (BVFs) and then Close-up-View Frontiers (CVFs) per BVF; the MLLM picks a BVF, then a CVF within it, each rendered as a snapshot facing the frontier cell.
Termination/answering: follows 3D-Mem's memory snapshots (filtered by question-relevant object categories) to decide when to answer; snapshots are not used for navigation.

setting.backbone: Qwen2.5-VL-type open-source MLLM and GPT-4o (frozen, prompted); the paper's macros hide exact model names
setting.training_data: none (training-free); an experience library is built from rollouts on the training splits (A-EQA: 164 tasks over 52 environments per the text; GOAT-Bench: 255 subtasks in 34 train scenes)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (RGB snapshots to MLLM; depth for TSDF/occupancy mapping and 3D object lifting)
setting.action_space: frontier selection (hierarchical BVF then CVF) executed by a shortest-path planner; 50-step budget
setting.privileged: none at test time; experience set built from training-split rollouts with outcomes

numbers_note: The A-EQA benchmark is entered as OpenEQA; the split is nominally the val set. Retrieval-versus-random, experience-quality, BVF/CVF-stage and candidate-count comparisons are given only in figures.
results: On A-EQA, ReEXplore with Qwen raises LLM-Match from 39.1 to 46.2, SR from 50.9 to 58.5 and SPL from 36.4 to 52.9 over 3D-Mem. With GPT-4o it reaches 58.3 LLM-Match and 75.5 SR versus 54.4 and 69.6 for 3D-Mem. On GOAT-Bench with Qwen it beats 3D-Mem (SR 53.2 vs 49.4, SPL 32.6 vs 20.7), but with GPT-4o it trails 3D-Mem (59.8/42.5 vs 65.1/49.3).
limitations: The evaluation is tiny (41 A-EQA questions, 278 GOAT subtasks), with no variance or significance reported.
It underperforms 3D-Mem on GOAT-Bench with GPT-4o, and language-description goals gain little; the authors attribute this to no prompt tuning.

It is tested only in indoor Habitat/HM3D simulation, with no outdoor or real-robot experiments; it also needs a prior experience set with outcomes and relies on 3D-Mem's snapshot mechanism for termination.
